title: How I got here
lead: My career started behind a front desk, not behind a code editor. Technology came later, and it came because of what I saw from there.

story.title: Hospitality
paragraphs: I have spent years working face to face with guests in accommodation: hotels, an apart-hotel and, earlier, corporate reception at Dorna Sports during MotoGP World Championship seasons. I have handled check-ins and check-outs, managed reservations and amendments, and looked after individual guests, groups, professional sports teams and international sponsors.
That work taught me to move between languages, to handle incidents calmly, and to understand that behind every booking there is a person with specific expectations.

story.title: Operations
paragraphs: Over time I moved from the front desk into how the property works behind the scenes: availability, room allocation, channel management, invoicing, coordination between departments and pricing operations.

Working with Booking.com, Expedia, direct sales and PMS such as Opera or Avalon gave me a very concrete perspective: I know what breaks in the operation when a tool fails, and I know what the front desk needs to be able to do its job.

story.title: Technology
paragraphs: In parallel I studied a Higher Vocational Qualification in Web Application Development and started building real software: first at Dorna Sports as a web development intern, then as a freelancer for Acerko.com and, above all, with Tanya Martelli Photography, a product I have been developing and maintaining since 2024.
I do not present myself as a senior engineer. I present myself as someone with technical training and real experience building and maintaining web products in production.

bridge.title: Why both halves belong together
paragraphs: I understand the problems of people who use hotel software because I have worked in the processes and with the tools used at the front desk every day. And I have enough technical grounding to talk to a product or engineering team about what can be built, how it integrates and why something fails.
That is useful wherever someone has to translate between what operations needs and what the product can do: implementation, onboarding, technical support, customer success or product in hotel tech.

items.title: Real operational context
items.text: I have worked in reception and in operations, so I understand the daily reality of the people who use the software, not just the demo.

items.title: A bridge between client and engineering
items.text: I can talk to the front desk and to developers and have both understand the same thing.

items.title: Ability to build
items.text: I do not just spot the problem: I can put together a prototype, integrate an API or maintain a product in production.
